Appendix P — Mobile-Dipole Field: Derivation, Controls, Reproduction and Handoff

P.1. Exact reduced variables and why the momentum is conserved

The A-05g model is a periodic, finite-Fourier-mode classical Hamiltonian. Retained degrees of freedom are Ak,ΠA,k,ψk,Πψ,kA_k,\Pi_{A,k},\psi_k,\Pi_{\psi,k} and two sets of (Xi,pXi,qi,pqi)(X_i,p_{X_i},q_i,p_{q_i}). Finite-width kernels have modal multipliers exp[−(kσ)2/2]\exp[-(k\sigma)^2/2]. The energy in (J1) is nonnegative when the stated response/stiffness inequalities hold. The optical and scalar response laws are modeling choices, not observational findings.

For a field f(x)=f0+∑k=1K(ckcoskx+sksinkx)f(x)=f_0+\sum_{k=1}^K(c_k\cos kx+s_k\sin kx) on L=2πL=2\pi (with the corresponding 2π/L2\pi/L factors for general LL), the normalized kernel sample is

f¯(X)=f0+∑k=1Ke−k2σ2/2[ckcos(kX)+sksin(kX)]. \overline f(X)=f_0+\sum_{k=1}^K e^{-k^2\sigma^2/2}[c_k\cos(kX)+s_k\sin(kX)]. \tag{App-P1}

The same kernel and the same spatial derivative of the sample are used for both the field-source terms and the material forces. Its use permits an exact continuous-translation symmetry of the truncated Hamiltonian; the polynomial field products are projected by a quadrature with sufficient nodes to avoid aliasing of the retained cubic terms. Under f(x)↦f(x−δ)f(x)\mapsto f(x-\delta), Xi↦Xi+δX_i\mapsto X_i+\delta, all terms in (J1) are invariant. Noether’s canonical generator is (J6). Any change in the total momentum is numerical integration error, not a hidden fixed support.

The internal coordinate qiq_i is transverse electric polarization; it is not the orbital position of a resolved three-dimensional electron. Its kinetic term has reduced mass mqm_q, and the longitudinal mechanical motion of the composite is described by XiX_i and inertial mass MM. Thus each composite is longitudinally mobile, but individual nucleons and electrons do not yet have full three-dimensional trajectories. This keeps the model honest about what is and is not closed.

P.2. Conjugate equations, screening and numerical initial conditions

Hamiltonian derivatives give (J3)–(J5). The scalar’s initial equilibrium solves, in the retained Fourier basis,

[−w2∂x2+mψ2]ψ0+∑i[hψ¯0(Xi)+12k0sqi2]Wσ(x−Xi)=mψ2ψ∞. \big[-w^2\partial_x^2+m_\psi^2\big]\psi_0 +\sum_i\left[h\overline\psi_0(X_i) +\tfrac12k_0s q_i^2\right]W_\sigma(x-X_i) =m_\psi^2\psi_\infty. \tag{App-P2}

The initial electromagnetic field and both field momenta are zero; the source is displaced and the receiver is unexcited. Every point-sample source is projected with the canonical modal normalization. Both centers’ initial mechanical momenta follow from their stated masses and velocities. No field is manually given an energy loss or an arbitrary driver after initialization.

The integration uses SciPy solve_ivp(..., method='DOP853', rtol=2e-10, atol=2e-12) with 301 saved times. The baseline has K=10K=10 positive harmonics and N=96N=96 quadrature sites. The higher-resolution run uses K=14K=14 and N=112N=112; the spatial smoothing width is unchanged. Both are within the alias-free quadrature condition N>6KN>6K. Periodic boundaries are a numerical simplification and do not represent unbounded intergalactic propagation.

P.3. Recorded tests and internal limits

The project suite now passes 196 tests, including 16 new tests dedicated to A-05g. These cover autonomous equations, positive energy and response coefficients, the initial static screening residual, no-source/no-coupling null controls, nonzero recoil for an initially resting center, energy and momentum invariance, exact translation invariance of HH and PP, covariance of the evolution laws under common spatial translation, field–charge coupling consistency, and directional derivatives of the two conservation generators.

The baseline maximum relative energy drift is 4.5598×10−114.5598\times10^{-11}, the maximum absolute momentum drift is 6.5861×10−136.5861\times10^{-13}, and the peak receiver displacement is 0.052079700.05207970 (dimensionless). The initial and final ratios of locally calibrated small-amplitude charge frequencies are 1.002825341.00282534 and 0.999807840.99980784, respectively. The higher-resolution receiver peak is 0.052079700.05207970 as well, differing by about 1.0×10−91.0\times10^{-9}. These simulation outputs do not measure an atomic line, a physical photon rest mass, or a cosmic distance.

The finite-mode model has no strict finite-support wavefront, and the Gaussian source kernel has instantaneous mathematical tails. The one-dimensional transverse current is a gauge-fixed approximation; longitudinal electric fields, full three-dimensional charge continuity, individually mobile negative and positive particles, radiative damping in open space, quantum transitions, gravity, and external astronomical observations are absent. The claimed conservation is of reduced canonical longitudinal momentum, not a verified tensor law for all electromagnetic matter in three dimensions. A static or local oscillator ratio is not by itself observed redshift.

The initial scalar modes are not set to zero arbitrarily. At the actual initial particle locations the stationary profile minimizes the scalar part of the Hamiltonian: if 𝐛i\mathbf b_i denotes the vector of all real Gaussian-smoothed basis components and Ω2\Omega^2 is diagonal in the modes,

[Ω2+∑isi𝐛i𝐛iT]𝐮0=−∑igi𝐛i,𝚷ψ,0=𝟎. \left[\Omega^2+\sum_is_i\mathbf b_i\mathbf b_i^T\right]\mathbf u_0 =-\sum_ig_i\mathbf b_i, \qquad\boldsymbol\Pi_{\psi,0}=\mathbf{0}. \tag{App-Q4}

Q.3. Three kinds of accuracy must not be confused

  1. Identity and constraint closure: (K5) and (K6) hold to floating-point precision on the retained modes, because both use identical deposition, and (K7) follows from translation symmetry. This is an analytical property of the truncated equations. The saved numerical residuals are roughly 10−1710^{-17}.
  2. Time integration accuracy: energy and momentum have numerical drifts ranging approximately from 10−1310^{-13} to 10−810^{-8} relative energy and up to about 2×10−112\times10^{-11} absolute canonical momentum over the recorded controls. These demonstrate high precision for the specified ODEs, not physical fidelity of an untested coupling.
  3. Spectral convergence: despite the first two successes, the matched-four-unit receiver response changes about 24.8% between 13 and 62 modes. Thus no stable quantitative receiver-response prediction or inferred astronomical parameter is warranted. Better mode/width/boundary convergence is an explicit acceptance condition for A-05i.

A periodic Coulomb-gauge truncation is not a numerical demonstration of exact free-space causal support. Gaussian kernels have tails. The instantaneous longitudinal solution implements a constraint, not superluminal physical signaling. The model does not independently derive ϵ(ψ)\epsilon(\psi) or μ(ψ)\mu(\psi), and does not test slowing light over cosmic progression. Neither its oscillator radiation nor a harmonic oscillator quantum analogy is a measured atomic line. There is no photon invariant rest mass term, experimentally detected scalar, astrophysical inference or peer-reviewed validation in this experiment.

Appendix R — Massive-Vector Derivation, Reproduction, and Source Concordance

Source of the proposed model: ArcSecs Scientific Investigation, Part XIX: Gauge-Invariant Massive Photons, Environmental Scalar Coupling, and the Electrostatic Screening Constraint, uploaded 23 November 2026. Preserved in docs/long-term-memory/research/massive-photon-field/part-xix-source.md without altering reports R01–R41. Part XIX originally labels its equations (600)–(619). Chapter 30L adopts its relevant field expressions under labels (L1)–(L9) and adds (L10)–(L11) as explicit consistency consequences.

R.1. The longitudinal constraint must be eliminated correctly

For homogeneous coefficients, choose the gauge χ=0\chi=0 and a Fourier mode with 𝐀L=AL𝐤̂\mathbf A_L=A_L\hat{\mathbf k}. Its quadratic Lagrangian is

LL=ϵ2(ȦL+kφ)2+ζ2φ2−η2AL2. L_L=\frac\epsilon2(\dot A_L+k\varphi)^2+\frac\zeta2\varphi^2-\frac\eta2 A_L^2. \tag{R1}

Variation with respect to the nondynamical φ\varphi gives φ=−ϵkȦL/(ϵk2+ζ)\varphi=-\epsilon k\dot A_L/(\epsilon k^2+\zeta). Substitution produces

LL=12ϵζϵk2+ζȦL2−η2AL2,ωL2=ηζk2+ηϵ. L_L=\frac12\frac{\epsilon\zeta}{\epsilon k^2+\zeta}\dot A_L^2-\frac\eta2 A_L^2, \quad \omega_L^2=\frac\eta\zeta k^2+\frac\eta\epsilon. \tag{R2}

The transverse modes instead obey ωT2=(bk2+η)/ϵ\omega_T^2=(bk^2+\eta)/\epsilon. The equality ωT2=ωL2\omega_T^2=\omega_L^2 for all kk demands η/ζ=b/ϵ\eta/\zeta=b/\epsilon (not merely equality of the gap at k=0k=0). The sign conditions guarantee positive reduced quadratic kinetic/potential coefficients, but no claim about global nonlinear stability follows. At vanishing vector mass the constraint structure changes; do not infer the longitudinal degree of freedom survives continuously as a propagating physical vacuum photon in that limit.

R.2. Static potential and frequency transport probe different mechanisms

The static sourced mode satisfies (∇2−ℓY−2)φ=−Qδ3(𝐫)/ϵ(\nabla^2-\ell_Y^{-2})\varphi=-Q\delta^3(\mathbf r)/\epsilon. Its decaying solution is φ=Qe−r/ℓY/(4πϵr)\varphi=Qe^{-r/\ell_Y}/(4\pi\epsilon r), with ℓY=ϵ/ζ\ell_Y=\sqrt{\epsilon/\zeta}. For the matched mode model, ℓY=cγ/Ωγ\ell_Y=c_\gamma/\Omega_\gamma. The relationship follows algebraically from the same coefficients that govern propagation; it is not an independently adjustable phenomenological correction.

For a homogeneous scalar history with constant gap Ω0\Omega_0, ω2(T,k)=cγ(T)2k2+Ω02\omega^2(T,k)=c_\gamma(T)^2k^2+\Omega_0^2. At fixed conserved wavevector kk,

∂Tlnω=cγ2k2cγ2k2+Ω02∂Tlncγ. \partial_T\ln\omega=\frac{c_\gamma^2k^2}{c_\gamma^2k^2+\Omega_0^2}\,\partial_T\ln c_\gamma. \tag{R3}

At fixed ω\omega in a stationary, spatially inhomogeneous background, the local wavenumber instead adapts to the profile. Stationary refraction and temporal energy exchange therefore predict distinct observations. For ω\omega below the local mass gap, the simple homogeneous propagating mode has no real wavenumber; a fully coupled boundary model must treat evanescence, polarization mixing, charge response and reflections rather than applying geometric optics mechanically.

The independent code tools/stueckelberg_scalar_v1.py evolves Hamiltonian canonical variables (ψ,pψ,AT,pT,AL,pL)(\psi,p_\psi,A_T,p_T,A_L,p_L) with the autonomous Hamiltonian

H=pψ22K+V(ψ)+pT22ϵ+bk2+η2AT2+pL22KL+η2AL2. H=\frac{p_\psi^2}{2K}+V(\psi) +\frac{p_T^2}{2\epsilon}+\frac{b k^2+\eta}{2}A_T^2 +\frac{p_L^2}{2K_L}+\frac\eta2 A_L^2. \tag{R4}

R.4. Where the new candidate cannot yet be merged into the existing 3D code

Chapter 30K employs finitely many Coulomb-gauge modes plus a retained longitudinal constraint, with conserved mode-projected charge and momentum. Part XIX introduces a propagating longitudinal polarization of a positive-mass vector. Converting one into the other is not a matter of replacing a dispersion formula in a plotting routine: both the longitudinal kinetic variable and the correct φ\varphi constraint must enter the Hamiltonian, and spatially varying ϵ,b,ζ,η\epsilon,b,\zeta,\eta must carry their own momentum and scalar backreaction.

The six-run Chapter 30K convergence failure remains in force. A defensible merger must (1) provide an explicit charged-matter/current action; (2) solve the Gauss constraint with finite-mass terms; (3) demonstrate charge continuity and three-momentum conservation again; (4) reproduce localized source/receiver observables under increasing Fourier cutoff; (5) compute quantum bound-state differences without interpreting a uniform potential offset as a spectral line shift; and (6) freeze parameter values before astronomical comparisons. A failure of these coefficients is a model failure, not a logical disproof of the twelve authorial ArcSecs premises.

R.5. Source-status and citation routing

The Part XIX source is a theoretical derivation, not a peer-reviewed result. Its references include an established Stueckelberg review (Ruegg and Ruiz-Altaba, arXiv:hep-th/0304245), a 2026 published radio-burst mass-bound study (Zhang et al., Physical Review D 113, 043513, DOI 10.1103/sh7h-94jy), a November 2026 published environmental-Higgs investigation (Gruzinov, Hook and Huang, Journal of High Energy Physics, DOI 10.1007/JHEP11(2026)186), and a distance-duality article accepted 13 November 2026 (Melchiorri, DOI 10.1103/2glj-ljfh). These external sources concern bounds and competing mechanism proposals; none measures an ArcSecs scalar, establishes cosmic photon deceleration, or supplies a quantitative fit of the chapter’s model. Keep existing observational constraints visible rather than fitting them away.

Appendix S — Bounded A-05j Source/Atom Derivation, Numerical Validation, and Reproduction

This appendix reports independently checked consequences of the Part XIX massive-vector action as incorporated in Chapter 30L, not a new measurement. The authoritative ArcSecs 12-principle charter remains .uai/totem.uai. The source research corpus R01–R41 is not rewritten. Equation labels (M1)–(M10) belong to Chapter 30M and do not renumber Part XIX’s archival equations. The unrelated Appendix M equation is labeled (App-M1).

S.1. Modewise continuity and its limits

For a smearing kernel GσG_\sigma independent of time and a signed set of constant charges, ρ̇=∑iqi[−𝐯i⋅∇Gσ(𝐱−𝐫i)]\dot\rho=\sum_i q_i[-\mathbf v_i\cdot\nabla G_\sigma(\mathbf x-\mathbf r_i)]. With 𝐣=∑iqi𝐯iGσ\mathbf j=\sum_iq_i\mathbf v_iG_\sigma, ∇⋅𝐣=∑iqi𝐯i⋅∇Gσ\nabla\cdot\mathbf j=\sum_iq_i\mathbf v_i\cdot\nabla G_\sigma. Hence ρ̇+∇⋅𝐣=0\dot\rho+\nabla\cdot\mathbf j=0 identically, including at every retained Fourier 𝐤\mathbf k when identical convolution weights are used. A different smoothing kernel or inconsistent charge interpolation for current and density would break this exact identity. If charges can change with time, additional source/sink currents must be modeled.

For the homogeneous Stueckelberg coefficients, the static potential mode satisfies (ϵk2+ζ)φ𝐤=ρ𝐤(\epsilon k^2+\zeta)\varphi_{\mathbf k}=\rho_{\mathbf k}. The numerical gauge-constraint test reproduces the source to floating-point precision and checks positivity of both coefficients. It is not evidence of stability of the full nonlinear time-dependent scalar/vector/matter field theory. The dynamic Hamiltonian and the longitudinal sector still require explicit implementation with those source terms.

The static force between two charges q1,q2q_1,q_2 at separation rr is, in the positive radial direction,

Fr=q1q24πϵe−r/ℓY(1r2+1ℓYr). F_r=\frac{q_1q_2}{4\pi\epsilon}e^{-r/\ell_Y} \left(\frac1{r^2}+\frac1{\ell_Yr}\right). \tag{S1}

It recovers Coulomb’s radial force as ℓY→∞\ell_Y\to\infty and agrees with a finite-difference derivative of the screened interaction potential. Agreement is internal to the model.

S.2. Quantum reference problem and perturbative integrals

The relative electron–nucleus Schrödinger equation in Chapter 30M uses x=r/aBx=r/a_B and ER=ℏ2/(2μraB2)E_R=\hbar^2/(2\mu_ra_B^2). Its dimensionless radial operator is −d2/dx2+l(l+1)/x2−2e−sx/x-d^2/dx^2+l(l+1)/x^2-2e^{-sx}/x. It is a one-particle central-potential model. The heavy nucleus approximation, absence of spin and self-energy, and homogeneity of the field over atomic distances must be included in any experimental comparison.

For normalized unscreened hydrogenic wavefunctions, ⟨e−sx/x⟩1s=4/(2+s)2\langle e^{-sx}/x\rangle_{1s}=4/(2+s)^2, ⟨e−sx/x⟩2s=1/[2(1+s)2]−1/(1+s)3+3/[4(1+s)4]\langle e^{-sx}/x\rangle_{2s}=1/[2(1+s)^2]-1/(1+s)^3+3/[4(1+s)^4], and ⟨e−sx/x⟩2p=1/[4(1+s)4]\langle e^{-sx}/x\rangle_{2p}=1/[4(1+s)^4]. The first-order shift 2[⟨1/x⟩−⟨e−sx/x⟩]2[\langle 1/x\rangle-\langle e^{-sx}/x\rangle] must be applied to each level before forming a transition. Its common order-ss term cancels in the difference; the splitting of the originally degenerate 2s2s and 2p2p levels begins at order s2s^2.

At s=0s=0 the exact reference has E1s=−1ERE_{1s}=-1E_R and E2s=E2p=−0.25ERE_{2s}=E_{2p}=-0.25E_R. The radial finite-difference operator is the symmetric three-diagonal matrix with diagonal 2/h2+l(l+1)/xj2−2e−sxj/xj2/h^2+l(l+1)/x_j^2-2e^{-sx_j}/x_j and nearest off-diagonal −1/h2-1/h^2. Dirichlet conditions at x=0x=0 and x=60x=60 implement a finite-box approximation; any residual box truncation has to be tested separately for extremely weak binding.

Appendix T — Quantum Receiver Hamiltonian, Cutoff Protocol, and Reproducibility Ledger

This appendix is the executable specification of Chapter 30N, Candidate A-05j Stage 2A. The word convergence refers here only to a declared observable in a declared one-dimensional, transverse, finite-width and two-level model. The authoritative twelve-principle ArcSecs charter is .uai/totem.uai. Archived R01–R41 reports, the original Part XIX manuscript, and the prior Chapter 30K unresolved cutoff finding remain untouched.

T.1. Positivity and dispersion

The field sector uses ϵ=eλψ>0\epsilon=e^{\lambda\psi}>0, bem=e−λψ>0b_{\mathrm{em}}=e^{-\lambda\psi}>0, η=Ω02eλψ>0\eta=\Omega_0^2e^{\lambda\psi}>0, with Fourier Cn=bemkn2+ηC_n=b_{\mathrm{em}}k_n^2+\eta. Its transverse characteristic speed is cT=e−λψc_T=e^{-\lambda\psi} and its positive mode frequency gap is Ω0\Omega_0. For kn>0k_n>0 the phase and group speeds differ:

ωn=cT2kn2+Ω02,vgroup=cT2knωn,vphase=ωnkn. \omega_n=\sqrt{c_T^2k_n^2+\Omega_0^2},\qquad v_{\mathrm{group}}=\frac{c_T^2k_n}{\omega_n},\qquad v_{\mathrm{phase}}=\frac{\omega_n}{k_n}. \tag{T1}

No longitudinal electromagnetic mode is evolved in this appendix. Stating the matched dispersion of an unimplemented longitudinal sector would not establish that sector’s dynamical constraint stability or its coupling to the moving quantum sources.

T.2. A single energy and momentum accounting convention

The implemented code specifies the quantum–classical energy as HH in (N3) and evolves both matter and fields from its Hamiltonian derivatives. For the atom’s internal two-level degree of freedom, Hj=Δj(I−σz)/2−gjA(Xj)σxH_j=\Delta_j(I-\sigma_z)/2-g_jA(X_j)\sigma_x. Its expectation generates (N5). Translating both centers and the field by the same increment leaves HH unchanged; with the cosine–sine Fourier convention of (N1), this yields the Noether momentum (N8). The code checks HH, PtotalP_{\mathrm{total}}, and the two Bloch norms separately at every recorded time.

The scalar equation includes a gap derivative Δ′(ψ)\Delta'(\psi); omitting it would create spurious energy when atomic calibration changed. The mode kinetic term includes ϵ′(ψ)\epsilon'(\psi) and the restoring term includes Cn′(ψ)C_n'(\psi). A finite-difference test independently checks derivatives of HH with respect to the scalar coordinate, a material center coordinate and a field-mode coordinate. The atom’s simulated two-level amplitudes satisfy u2+v2+w2=1u^2+v^2+w^2=1 by construction up to numerical error.

T.3. Source and detector states

The source is prepared in a coherent superposition with (us,vs,ws)=(1,0,0)(u_s,v_s,w_s)=(1,0,0), the receiver in its ground state (ur,vr,wr)=(0,0,1)(u_r,v_r,w_r)=(0,0,1), and all transverse Fourier field amplitudes zero. This initial source state has a nonzero dipole expectation. A pure excited state (0,0,−1)(0,0,-1) with exactly zero classical field gives no emission in the semiclassical model; tests explicitly preserve this limitation. Physical spontaneous emission requires a different quantum field state, vacuum fluctuations, or a more complete model.

The receiver observable is 𝒫r(T)=(1−wr(T))/2\mathcal P_r(T)=(1-w_r(T))/2. The quoted spectrum-proxy value at detuning δ\delta is maxT≥Tarrival+2𝒫r(T)\max_{T\ge T_{\mathrm{arrival}}+2}\mathcal P_r(T), with Tarrival=(Xr−Xs)/exp(−λψ(0))T_{\mathrm{arrival}}=(X_r-X_s)/\exp(-\lambda\psi(0)) used only to establish a common post-arrival window. The evolving group velocity is frequency dependent because Ω0>0\Omega_0>0, so this fixed geometric reference is not a computed wave-packet arrival time. A finite-time excitation-vs-detuning scan is not interchangeable with a spectrometer’s photon-energy distribution.

T.4. The screened-atom input is a local surrogate

The Chapter 30M reference 𝒟0≃0.742152\mathcal D_0\simeq0.742152 at s0=0.05s_0=0.05 is imported as a computed scalar reference. The derivative 𝒟′pert(s0)≃−0.29014649\mathcal D'_{\mathrm{pert}}(s_0)\simeq-0.29014649 comes from the first-order unscreened-hydrogenic perturbation formula, not the derivative of the converged finite-screening eigenproblem. In (N4), the Yukawa parameter s=s0e2λψs=s_0e^{2\lambda\psi} stays approximately 0.0510.051–0.0520.052 in the main runs. The resulting change in gap is a defined, local extrapolation; it does not derive a dynamical quantum atomic wavefunction under time-varying scalar gradients.

The scalar starts at ψ=0.04\psi=0.04 and responds to the shared Hamiltonian (N3), rather than being prescribed by hand. Under the baseline parameters its recorded value lies approximately in [0.0398,0.0767][0.0398,0.0767] and the receiver gap lies approximately in [0.71369,0.72725][0.71369,0.72725] in dimensionless units. Those are simulation outputs, not new measurements of fundamental-constant drift.

T.7. Why the next model remains difficult

The full acceptance gate continues to require a consistent three-dimensional action for signed mobile charges, atom/nucleus center-of-mass motion, a gauge-complete Stueckelberg longitudinal mode with its scalar-potential constraint, all transverse radiative modes, spatial scalar screening and dynamic microscopic transition matrix elements. It must demonstrate simultaneously: charge continuity, Gauss-law residual convergence, all energy/momentum ledgers, a cutoff-stable and physically regularized receiver line shape, and a frozen-parameter observational comparison. Chapter 30N supplies a transparent working receiver benchmark for that future effort; it does not substitute for it.

Appendix U — Three-Dimensional Charge-Conserving Green Response: Derivation and Reproduction Ledger

This appendix contains the complete executable specification for Chapter 30O, Candidate A-05j-B. All quantities in the numerical examples are dimensionless. It follows the Chapter 30L and Part XIX massive-vector action; neither a gravitational-wave action nor a time-varying scalar is included. The results are mathematically derived or simulated, never presented as an astronomical observation.

U.1. Fourier and gauge conventions

Use a cubic periodic box of side LL with 𝐤=(2π/L)(nx,ny,nz)\mathbf k=(2\pi/L)(n_x,n_y,n_z) and the convention f(𝐱)=L−3∑𝐤f𝐤ei𝐤⋅𝐱f(\mathbf x)=L^{-3}\sum_{\mathbf k}f_{\mathbf k}e^{i\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf x}. Time-harmonic factors are written e−izTe^{-izT}, with z=ω+iγz=\omega+i\gamma used only to evaluate the retarded complex-frequency response. For physical real driving, the actual field is obtained from a suitable inverse frequency transform. Here γ>0\gamma>0 is a fixed broadening/window parameter, not the dissipation coefficient of a coupled energy-conserving system.

The vector action is (O1) with its massive χ\chi gauge redundancy; the sources obey charge conservation. In unitary gauge χ=0\chi=0, the Fourier field equations can be checked independently as

[(−ϵz2+η+bk2)I−b𝐤𝐤T]𝐀+ϵz𝐤φ=𝐉,−ϵz𝐤⋅𝐀+(ϵk2+ζ)φ=ρ. \begin{aligned} \big[(-\epsilon z^2+\eta+b k^2)I-b\mathbf k\mathbf k^T\big]\mathbf A +\epsilon z\mathbf k\varphi&=\mathbf J,\\ -\epsilon z\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf A+(\epsilon k^2+\zeta)\varphi&=\rho. \end{aligned}\tag{U1}

The second line is the modified Gauss constraint, not an optional extra propagation mode. With b/ϵ=η/ζ=cγ2b/\epsilon=\eta/\zeta=c_\gamma^2 and η/ϵ=Ωγ2\eta/\epsilon=\Omega_\gamma^2, the 4×44\times4 system produces (O4). This provides two implementations of the same theory: (i) the derived compact Green expression and (ii) a direct matrix solution with no projector substitutions. Their agreement is an algebraic cross-check rather than an independent physical observation.

U.2. Positive and negative cloud source

Let gσ(𝐱−𝐗)g_\sigma(\mathbf x-\mathbf X) be a normalized periodic Gaussian (specified via Fourier coefficients e−σ2k2/2e−i𝐤⋅𝐗e^{-\sigma^2k^2/2}e^{-i\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf X}). With charges +q+q and −q-q and positions 𝐗±𝐝/2\mathbf X\pm\mathbf d/2, the exact expressions for ρ𝐤\rho_{\mathbf k} and 𝐉𝐤\mathbf J_{\mathbf k} are given in (O3). Direct differentiation yields

ρ̇𝐤=−iqGse−i𝐤⋅𝐗cos(𝐤⋅𝐝/2)(𝐤⋅𝐝̇),i𝐤⋅𝐉𝐤=−ρ̇𝐤. \dot\rho_{\mathbf k}=-iq\,G_s e^{-i\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf X} \cos(\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf d/2)(\mathbf k\cdot\dot{\mathbf d}), \qquad i\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf J_{\mathbf k}=-\dot\rho_{\mathbf k}.\tag{U2}

The exact formula assumes the center 𝐗\mathbf X is fixed. A moving center would require its own current term; a future fully dynamical implementation must include it. In the small-separation limit, 𝐩=q𝐝\mathbf p=q\mathbf d, ρ𝐤=−i𝐤⋅𝐩Gs\rho_{\mathbf k}=-i\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf p\,G_s and 𝐉𝐤=𝐩̇Gs\mathbf J_{\mathbf k}=\dot{\mathbf p}\,G_s. The harmonic transfer formula uses this linear limit, not the full nonlinear two-cloud source. The exact pair formula is tested separately to guard charge continuity outside the linear approximation.

U.3. Receiver quantity and convergence metric

The computed receiver is not a quantum sensor population. It is the signed, complex field average in (O6). The yy-polarized emitter has unit dipole axis and the receiver projects along yy. At each frequency ωj\omega_j and cutoff NN, compute both the real and imaginary parts of HNH_N. The acceptance metric is

𝒞N,N′=maxj|HN(ωj+iγ)−HN′(ωj+iγ)|max(|HN′(ωj+iγ)|,10−14). \mathcal C_{N,N'}=\max_j\frac{|H_N(\omega_j+i\gamma)-H_{N'}(\omega_j+i\gamma)|} {\max(|H_{N'}(\omega_j+i\gamma)|,10^{-14})}.\tag{U3}

The denominator floor is declared and not tuned from the results. This measure captures phase and amplitude. In the baseline example, 𝒞10,12≤1.40×10−6\mathcal C_{10,12}\leq1.40\times10^{-6} across nine frequencies, and the largest absolute complex difference is 1.092×10−101.092\times10^{-10}. Both source and receiver Gaussian widths are held fixed throughout. The full three-dimensional Fourier counts are (2N+1)3(2N+1)^3, including the homogeneous mode. The k=0k=0 mode is included without defining a meaningless longitudinal direction at zero wavevector.

U.6. Boundaries of the result and next acceptance gate

The positive-gap matched massive-vector formalism is classical. A fixed scalar environment determines its coefficients; it does not solve a density-dependent screening boundary. A prescribed moving charge pair satisfies continuity but is not dynamically force-balanced by the field and is not assigned a closed mechanical/field energy ledger. The harmonic linearization cannot predict a true atomic source line, an excitation probability, spontaneous emission, photon counting, or astronomically measured redshift. Finite periodic boundary conditions and the selected complex-frequency window remain modeling choices. The previous Chapter 30K dynamical receiver’s approximately 25% cutoff discrepancy remains unresolved.

Required next test: replace prescribed dipole motion with self-consistent three-dimensional signed particle and bound-state motion; evolve the spatial scalar and longitudinal Stueckelberg constraint together with transverse radiation; independently check three-component momentum, charge continuity, Gauss law, energy exchange and a quantum receiver spectrum. Only after that spectrum converges at physically fixed, externally justified charge widths should model coefficients be frozen for observational testing. The twelve authorial foundations are held intact while candidate mathematical mechanisms are tested and, when necessary, rejected.

Appendix V — Charged Quantum Receiver: Hamiltonian Audit, Convergence and Reproduction

V.1. Scope and source concordance

This appendix documents the bounded Candidate A-05j-C calculation used in Chapter 30P. It combines mathematical elements from Chapter 30K (independent signed charge motion and canonical momentum), Chapter 30M (static Yukawa atomic gap), Chapter 30N (coherent two-level dynamics) and Chapter 30O (three-dimensional positive-gap massive-vector response and finite-width convergence). Each predecessor remains a separate source and its limitations remain in the book. The present reduced gauge-fixed Hamiltonian is not the complete four-potential Stueckelberg action of Chapter 30L/Part XIX.

V.2. Canonical construction

Particles are numbered i=1,…,4i=1,\ldots,4, with signed charges (+q,−q,+q,−q)(+q,-q,+q,-q). The positive and negative members of source and receiver each have independent three-dimensional position and canonical momentum. Choose the real half-lattice Fourier basis and the same Gaussian kernel for charge density, current and transverse vector potential. The canonical pairs are (𝐫i,𝐩i)(\mathbf r_i,\mathbf p_i), (a𝐤ℓc,s,π𝐤ℓc,s)(a^{c,s}_{\mathbf k\ell},\pi^{c,s}_{\mathbf k\ell}), and (ψ,pψ)(\psi,p_\psi). The two internal Bloch vectors obey the standard coherent-state spin Poisson bracket that gives (P3). The total Hamiltonian is (P2). There is no external forcing or time-dependent prescribed coefficient.

For ϵ=eλψ\epsilon=e^{\lambda\psi}, b=ϵ−1b=\epsilon^{-1}, η=Ω2ϵ\eta=\Omega^2\epsilon and ζ=Ω2ϵ3\zeta=\Omega^2\epsilon^3, the constrained screened electrostatic energy is

HL=12∑𝐤ρ𝐤,c2+ρ𝐤,s2ϵk2+ζ,∂HL∂ψ=−λ2∑𝐤(ρc2+ρs2)(ϵk2+3ζ)(ϵk2+ζ)2. H_L=\frac12\sum_{\mathbf k}\frac{\rho_{\mathbf k,c}^2+\rho_{\mathbf k,s}^2}{\epsilon k^2+\zeta},\qquad \frac{\partial H_L}{\partial\psi}=-\frac\lambda2\sum_{\mathbf k}\frac{(\rho_c^2+\rho_s^2)(\epsilon k^2+3\zeta)}{(\epsilon k^2+\zeta)^2}. \tag{V1}

The same ψ\psi derivatives of the transverse vector Hamiltonian and transition gaps are included in ṗψ=−∂H/∂ψ\dot p_\psi=-\partial H/\partial\psi. Omitting any of those reciprocal terms would break the energy ledger. For massive-vector electrostatic screening, ℓY=ϵ/ζ=1/(Ωϵ)\ell_Y=\sqrt{\epsilon/\zeta}=1/(\Omega\epsilon) in the normalized units of the chosen coefficient family. That is not a measured vacuum photon range.

V.3. Mode-projected conservation and reference tests

The charge deposition and current identity are (P4), and the reduced screened Gauss constraint is (ϵk2+ζ)φ𝐤=ρ𝐤(\epsilon k^2+\zeta)\varphi_{\mathbf k}=\rho_{\mathbf k}. Differentiate the energy and three momentum components along the full coupled ordinary differential equations: the result vanishes analytically within the finite basis. The Bloch unit norms satisfy 𝐬j⋅𝐬̇j=0\mathbf s_j\cdot\dot{\mathbf s}_j=0. An independent centered-difference calculation tests particle, scalar and vector canonical derivatives of HH without reusing each programmed force expression as its own validation. A simultaneous physical translation of charges and Fourier modes leaves HH and 𝐏\mathbf P unchanged.

Note the distinction between a Gauss constraint and a propagating longitudinal massive-vector mode. The first is present; the second is deliberately absent. The fixed-gauge dipole–vector term is not by itself a fundamental gauge-redundant matter coupling.

V.4. Frozen numerical protocol and outputs

The baseline uses L=14L=14, σ=1.75\sigma=1.75, Ω=0.40\Omega=0.40, λ=0.16\lambda=0.16, gs=gr=1.5g_s=g_r=1.5, signed charges ±0.24\pm0.24, scalar inertia Kψ=10K_\psi=10, scalar potential stiffness 1212, initial ψ=0.04\psi=0.04, and center separation 55. Run the DOP853 adaptive integrator with rtol=10−8\mathrm{rtol}=10^{-8}, atol=3×10−10\mathrm{atol}=3\times10^{-10}, maximum step 0.140.14, and 121 equally spaced output times over 0≤T≤120\leq T\leq12. These are numerical controls, not inferred universal constants. The initial source is a coherent Bloch superposition (1,0,0)(1,0,0), not a pure excited eigenstate; an unforced pure excited source has no coherent dipole expectation in this approximation.

The generated comparison.csv contains 14 simulations: shell cutoffs 1–5, source and receiver decoupling, constant electromagnetic/scalar coefficients, a wider physical charge kernel, zero explicit signed charge, and four independent receiver detunings. baseline_trace.csv stores the shell-4 receiver population, conserved quantities and scalar trajectory; summary.json mirrors the comparisons in machine-readable form. The figures are charged-quantum-3d-convergence.png, charged-quantum-3d-detuning.png, and charged-quantum-3d-trace.png.

The full test suite has 346 passing tests at this edition. No new R42 historical report is asserted.

V.6. Exact limitation and the next scientific decision

The calculation is a coherent mean-field two-level detector, not a realistic atomic Hamiltonian or a probability distribution from measured photon counts. Its signed particles use placeholder harmonic binding, and their screened Coulomb energy is mode-regularized. The scalar is homogeneous, whereas the historical chameleon-like research asks for true spatial screening. The longitudinal Stueckelberg physical mode, quantized radiation vacuum, spontaneous emission, fine-structure multiplets and gravitational interaction are absent. Convergence with respect to Fourier cutoff at one σ\sigma does not justify extrapolating σ→0\sigma\to0, changing the box, or identifying the calculated transition with observed hydrogen spectra. All astronomical and laboratory data are untouched in this appendix.

Next acceptance task: construct and validate a self-consistent spatial-scalar and propagating-longitudinal massive-vector matter action with a gauge-consistent dipole operator, then demonstrate independent three-dimensional detector convergence at a physically calibrated charge distribution. Preserve the failures of earlier candidate formulations and predeclare failure tolerances before observational fitting.

Appendix W — Screened Stueckelberg Boundary: Gauge, Energy, Scattering and Reproduction

Research record: 23 November 2026. This appendix documents the source-derived action, independent algebra, numerical normalization, controls, and open limitations of Chapter 30Q. All numbers are from a synthetic normalized model; no physical observation was fitted.

W.1. Physical degrees of freedom and the correct longitudinal elimination

The gauge-invariant construction is the positive-coefficient Stueckelberg action of original Part XIX, reproduced and distinguished in Chapter 30L. In a stratified, charge-free probe region, Ex=−Ȧx−φ′E_x=-\dot A_x-\varphi', D=ϵExD=\epsilon E_x and unitary gauge χ=0\chi=0. Treat φ\varphi as a constraint rather than a propagating independent field. Variation yields D′+ζφ=0D'+\zeta\varphi=0; variation of AxA_x gives Ḋ=ηAx\dot D=\eta A_x. Therefore φ=−D′/ζ\varphi=-D'/\zeta and Ax=Ḋ/ηA_x=\dot D/\eta, which imply

∂T(Ḋ/η)−∂x(D′/ζ)+D/ϵ=0. \partial_T(\dot D/\eta)-\partial_x(D'/\zeta)+D/\epsilon=0.\tag{W1}

By contrast, varying AyA_y yields ∂T(ϵȦy)−∂x(bAy′)+ηAy=0\partial_T(\epsilon\dot A_y)-\partial_x(bA_y')+\eta A_y=0. For the fixed coefficient profiles all terms in

HL=∫dx[Ḋ22η+(D′)22ζ+D22ϵ],HT=∫dx[ϵȦy22+b(Ay′)22+ηAy22] H_L=\int dx\left[\frac{\dot D^2}{2\eta}+\frac{(D')^2}{2\zeta}+\frac{D^2}{2\epsilon}\right], \quad H_T=\int dx\left[\frac{\epsilon\dot A_y^2}{2}+\frac{b(A_y')^2}{2}+\frac{\eta A_y^2}{2}\right]\tag{W2}

are nonnegative, and positive for nonzero finite-energy excitations. The associated fluxes are −ḊD′/ζ-\dot D D'/\zeta and −bȦyAy′-b\dot A_y A_y' respectively. A fixed material background can exchange momentum with waves, and the complete moving-matter momentum ledger is not included. The work done to establish a scalar profile is also outside this frozen-background wave experiment.

W.2. Exact scalar boundary solution and independent discrete solve

For |x|<a|x|<a, let ρ=ρi\rho=\rho_i; outside let ρ=ρo\rho=\rho_o. Define kj=(m2+gρj)/Sk_j=\sqrt{(m^2+g\rho_j)/S} and ψj*=f/(m2+gρj)\psi_j^*=f/(m^2+g\rho_j). Impose ψ(±L)=ψo*\psi(\pm L)=\psi_o^*, continuity of ψ\psi, and continuity of scalar gradient Sψ′S\psi' at x=±ax=\pm a. A parity-even exact solution is

ψ(x)={ψi*+Acosh(kix),|x|≤a,ψo*+Bsinh(ko(L−|x|)),a<|x|≤L, \psi(x)=\begin{cases} \psi_i^*+A\cosh(k_i x),&|x|\le a,\\ \psi_o^*+B\sinh(k_o(L-|x|)),&a<|x|\le L, \end{cases}\tag{W3}

with

A=ψo*−ψi*cosh(kia)+(ki/ko)sinh(kia)tanh[ko(L−a)],B=−Akisinh(kia)kocosh[ko(L−a)]. A=\frac{\psi_o^*-\psi_i^*}{\cosh(k_i a)+(k_i/k_o)\sinh(k_i a)\tanh[k_o(L-a)]}, \quad B=-\frac{Ak_i\sinh(k_i a)}{k_o\cosh[k_o(L-a)]}.\tag{W4}

An independent banded finite-difference solve approximates −Sψ″+(m2+gρ)ψ=f-S\psi''+(m^2+g\rho)\psi=f with the density averaged across each grid control cell at the sharp transition, rather than assigning an arbitrary node value to the discontinuity. Both solutions are saved and compared. This tests the field profile before it is used for scattering. The scattering code itself uses the exact profile so its grid refinement does not accidentally retune the density edge.

W.3. Matched modes can scatter differently

The coefficients ϵ=eθ\epsilon=e^\theta, b=e−θb=e^{-\theta}, η=Ω02eθ\eta=\Omega_0^2e^\theta, ζ=Ω02e3θ\zeta=\Omega_0^2e^{3\theta} yield c2=b/ϵ=η/ζ=e−2θc^2=b/\epsilon=\eta/\zeta=e^{-2\theta} and Ω2=η/ϵ=Ω02\Omega^2=\eta/\epsilon=\Omega_0^2. For a stationary Fourier frequency ω>Ω0\omega>\Omega_0, the canonical flux factor κs=psk\kappa_s=p_s k is

κT=ω2−Ω02,κL=e−2θΩ02ω2−Ω02. \kappa_T=\sqrt{\omega^2-\Omega_0^2},\quad \kappa_L=\frac{e^{-2\theta}}{\Omega_0^2}\sqrt{\omega^2-\Omega_0^2}.\tag{W5}

Continuity of usu_s and psus′p_su_s' across a sharp step yields rs=(κs1−κs2)/(κs1+κs2)r_s=(\kappa_{s1}-\kappa_{s2})/(\kappa_{s1}+\kappa_{s2}), hence rT=0r_T=0 but rL=tanh(θ2−θ1)r_L=\tanh(\theta_2-\theta_1). In a smooth slab, the transfer-matrix calculation multiplies exact constant-coefficient propagation matrices on each spatial cell:

(upsu′)x+Δx=(cos(kΔx)sin(kΔx)/(psk)−psksin(kΔx)cos(kΔx))(upsu′)x. \begin{pmatrix}u\\p_su'\end{pmatrix}_{x+\Delta x} =\begin{pmatrix} \cos(k\Delta x)&\sin(k\Delta x)/(p_sk)\\ -p_sk\sin(k\Delta x)&\cos(k\Delta x) \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix}u\\p_su'\end{pmatrix}_{x}.\tag{W6}

Its determinant is exactly one in algebra. Incident/reflected/outgoing boundary vectors give r,tr,t by a 2-by-2 complex solve. Flux conservation is independently checked as |r|2+(κR/κL)|t|2=1|r|^2+(\kappa_R/\kappa_L)|t|^2=1; this test does not assume that amplitudes are energy fractions. For the chosen symmetric slab, both exterior media are identical, making the flux prefactor one. This is a gauge-consistent one-dimensional normal-incidence solution, not a general 3D boundary condition for all gauge and material sectors.

W.4. A separate positive-energy time-domain solver

For fixed coefficients, both polarizations have equations q̈=−BCq\ddot q=-BCq with positive diagonal BB and symmetric positive stiffness matrix CC after flux-conserving central differencing. Choose canonical momentum p=B−1q̇p=B^{-1}\dot q; the discrete Hamiltonian is H=(Δx/2)(pTBp+qTCq)H=(\Delta x/2)(p^TBp+q^TCq). Implicit midpoint updates q,pq,p in a time-symmetric, quadratic-invariant-preserving system. The separate field-energy test reports relative drift about 10−1410^{-14} or better in the recorded demonstration. The solver does not evolve the matter source or the scalar background and thus cannot be cited as a complete matter–field exchange simulation.

W.6. Limits and the next falsifiable decision

This is a fixed, one-dimensional density-screened background, not a time-evolving chameleon backreacting to emitted radiation. Gauge invariance of the classical vector action does not itself supply a quantized atom or renormalizable microscopic matter sector. Transverse reflectionlessness relies on the special exponentially matched coefficients and normal incidence; the longitudinal reflected fraction depends on slab thickness, scalar gradient, frequency and reference parameters. The model does not predict the universe’s age, size, recession speed, astronomical redshift, standard-candle brightness, or real spectroscopic photon mass. Those remain separate physical and observational tasks.

The next planned test must dynamically evolve spatial ψ\psi, signed charges and all three vector polarizations with one conserved energy–momentum inventory, then achieve resolution-stable three-dimensional receiver spectra without recalibrating the physical charge distribution between cutoffs. Failure to meet any of those conditions must be reported explicitly; it cannot be hidden by the present successful linear boundary test.

Appendix X — Consolidated Paper Review, Independent Calculations and Source Ledger

Derivation and reproduction

The new PDF source is ArcSecs: A Physical-Process Research Program for Photon Propagation, Cosmic Distance, and Relational Inertia, review edition 1.0, 22 pages, archived unchanged as docs/long-term-memory/research/cosmic-aging/source-paper.pdf. The companion detailed review is docs/long-term-memory/research/cosmic-aging/review.md. The paper’s original companion code was not supplied. This appendix documents a separate implementation, not a rerun of that original code. No earlier numerical result is reclassified as measured data.

For (CR2), the shell field relative to its center is the angular integral

I(r)I(0)=eq2∫−11e−q1+x2−2xμ1+x2−2xμdμ.\frac{I(r)}{I(0)}=\frac{e^q}{2}\int_{-1}^{1}\frac{e^{-q\sqrt{1+x^2-2x\mu}}}{\sqrt{1+x^2-2x\mu}}\,d\mu.\tag{CX1}

Substituting the separation s=1+x2−2xμs=\sqrt{1+x^2-2x\mu} reduces the integral to a finite interval in ss and gives (CR2). A 30-case independent quadrature over six ranges and five radii agrees to maximum relative error 1.90×10−131.90\times10^{-13}. The derivative of the distance integral (CR4) is the stated packet velocity. Invert the energy ratio to obtain the dimensionless age

γτ=ln(1+z)+12ln1−ϵ21−ϵ2(1+z)2.\gamma\tau=\ln(1+z)+\tfrac12\ln\frac{1-\epsilon^2}{1-\epsilon^2(1+z)^2}.\tag{CX2}

A direct adaptive quadrature over 20 cases agrees with (CR4) to maximum absolute error 4.34×10−154.34\times10^{-15} in C/γC/\gamma units. Very small speed deficits are evaluated with (CR5), not by subtracting nearly equal machine-precision numbers. The exterior bound (CR6) follows by substituting the final dispersion in vf≤viv_f\le v_i. It is necessary only. For collinear momentum loss pi>pf≥0p_i>p_f\ge0, the released energy per net momentum is

E(pi)−E(pf)pi−pf=C2(pi+pf)E(pi)+E(pf)≤vi.\frac{E(p_i)-E(p_f)}{p_i-p_f}=\frac{C^2(p_i+p_f)}{E(p_i)+E(p_f)}\le v_i.\tag{CX3}

Therefore a bath whose possible excitations obey ΔEbath≥umin|Δp|\Delta E_{\mathrm{bath}}\ge u_{\min}|\Delta p| cannot receive the transferred momentum if umin>viu_{\min}>v_i. This is a conditional kinematic restriction, not a general no-drag theorem. A real bath can include recoil, other modes and additional degrees of freedom. Derive (CR7) by differentiating the arrival condition at fixed launch momentum, assuming a smooth first-arrival branch. A twelve-case finite-difference derivative check gives maximum discrepancy 7.78×10−117.78\times10^{-11}. No source-frame emission transformation, atomic state or bath is simulated in this benchmark.

The paper’s 1S–2S Yukawa coefficient can also be checked independently: expand −Ke−r/ℓ/r=−K/r+K/ℓ−Kr/(2ℓ2)+⋯-K e^{-r/\ell}/r=-K/r+K/\ell-Kr/(2\ell^2)+\cdots. The constant cancels; the hydrogenic radial means are 1.5aB1.5a_B and 6aB6a_B, while the Coulomb transition is 3K/(8aB)3K/(8a_B). The fractional leading shift is −6(aB/ℓ)2-6(a_B/\ell)^2 in this restricted nonrelativistic, fixed-coupling limit. This is not a full QED prediction.

Appendix Y — Bath Recoil, Scalar Phase Space, and Reproduction

Conservation and threshold derivation

Chapter 30S’s 𝐪=𝐩−𝐩′\mathbf q=\mathbf p-\mathbf p' fixes momentum in all three components by construction. For a selected allowed energy fraction, the computed vector norm is checked against the independently specified bath dispersion. The law of cosines gives (BS2) and the momentum triangle bounds; imposing an angular tolerance instead of the full triangle gives (BS3). To obtain (BS4), use the positive-energy relation E′=E−sqE'=E-sq in the acoustic limit, square it and subtract the initial dispersion. The surviving energy must remain positive. For 0<s<C0<s<C and q>0q>0, the right side of (BS4) increases with qq, so the largest allowed momentum lies at cosθb=1\cos\theta_b=1. The result (BS5) is below the energy-only bound and respects the positive-energy branch. This establishes a threshold in the linear acoustic limit, not a rate in a realistic medium. More generally the strict slope bound |dE/dp|<C|dE/dp|<C for positive mass and finite momentum implies |E(p)−E(p′)|<C|𝐩−𝐩′||E(p)-E(p')|< C|\mathbf p-\mathbf p'| whenever the momenta differ. Thus a bath costing at least CqCq cannot receive the emitted energy from this isolated two-body channel.

Scalar surrogate rate

The canonical scalar potential (BS10) expands to quadratic gaps, the cubic interaction gσa2/2g\sigma a^2/2, and a positive quartic g2a4/(8mb2)g^2a^4/(8m_b^2). This is a nonnegative classical Hamiltonian; no renormalized quantum stability result is claimed. With ℏ=C=1\hbar=C=1, the leading-order transition uses the mode normalization 1/2E1/\sqrt{2E} and 1/2B1/\sqrt{2B} from canonical kinetic terms. Before integrating the final-state momentum, the rate is

Γ=12E∫d3p′(2π)32E′d3q(2π)32B(2π)4g2δ(3)(𝐩−𝐩′−𝐪)δ(E−E′−B).\Gamma=\frac{1}{2E}\int\frac{d^3p'}{(2\pi)^3 2E'}\frac{d^3q}{(2\pi)^3 2B}\,(2\pi)^4g^2\delta^{(3)}(\mathbf p-\mathbf p'-\mathbf q)\delta(E-E'-B).\tag{App-Y1}

Integrate the three-momentum delta function, then the azimuth and the cosine of the emission angle. The Jacobian magnitude for the energy delta function is pq/E′pq/E'. It cancels the final packet factor 1/E′1/E' and gives

dΓdq=g216πEpqB(q).\frac{d\Gamma}{dq}=\frac{g^2}{16\pi Ep}\frac{q}{B(q)}.\tag{App-Y2}

The limits require that the cosine root be real. At fixed qq the least possible total final energy is (p−q)2+ma2+B(q)\sqrt{(p-q)^2+m_a^2}+B(q). The largest, reached with opposite momenta, is always greater than EE for q>0q>0. Hence the allowed qq interval is the sublevel set of a convex function. With ma,mb>0m_a,m_b>0, locate its minimum and then its two intersections with EE if the minimum is below EE. Use q≤(E−ma)2−mb2/sq\le \sqrt{(E-m_a)^2-m_b^2}/s as the energy-only upper endpoint. The solver is exercised away from degenerate thresholds, not a certified near-threshold root finder. Changing variables with dB/dq=s2q/BdB/dq=s^2q/B yields (BS11). The mean emitted energy is (B1+B2)/2(B_1+B_2)/2, and the leading loss power is this mean times Γ\Gamma. Direct adaptive quadrature of (App-Y2) and its energy-weighted form checks both analytic integrations. The scalar proxy is not the rate for the full vector action, and no radiation or absorption amplitude for atoms has been derived.

Conditional statistical models

The uniform azimuth average removes the transverse term in the update of the directional cosine, so conditional expectation iterates as ⟨cosΘj⟩=cosϕj⟨cosΘj−1⟩\langle\cos\Theta_j\rangle=\cos\phi_j\langle\cos\Theta_{j-1}\rangle. The Monte Carlo calculation independently rotates the direction cosine at each step using random azimuths. The small-angle, small-gap acoustic asymptote is ϕj≃fβ−2−1\phi_j\simeq f\sqrt{\beta^{-2}-1} at f≪1f\ll1, so σdir≃(ln2)β−2−1/N\sigma_{\mathrm{dir}}\simeq(\ln2)\sqrt{\beta^{-2}-1}/\sqrt{N}. This is the basis of the order-4.8×1094.8\times10^9 event-count extrapolation, not an experimental restriction. The line-noise result follows from the binomial generating function ⟨tK⟩=(1−πb+πbt)N\langle t^K\rangle=(1-\pi_b+\pi_b t)^N. Applying it to t=1−ft=1-f and t=(1−f)2t=(1-f)^2 supplies (BS7) and (BS8). Neither chosen schedule is the actual scalar-proxy emission process. For the positive-gap case, the last equal-log step is the most restrictive energy-only bound; setting its loss no lower than EbE_b gives (BS9).

Reproduction and acceptance record

Run python tools/bath_recoil_v1.py and python -m unittest discover -s tests -q from the project root. The output folder docs/long-term-memory/research/bath-recoil/ contains five CSV datasets (events.csv, bands.csv, cascades.csv, linewidth.csv, scalar-rates.csv), and verification.txt. The program regenerates both figures. The event scan has 24 parameter cases (forbidden triangles are recorded explicitly); allowed-speed bands cover 48 cases, the directional cascade has six event counts, the line-noise study seven slot counts, and the positive-gap scalar rate scan 27 cases. All are synthetic. The largest tested allowed-event energy or momentum-magnitude residual is 3.33×10−163.33\times10^{-16} in the normalized units. The three-vector conservation is built into event reconstruction, not a long-time integration of interacting fields. The azimuth ensemble uses 20,000 independent draws per case and seed 3026. The 29 new tests cover allowed/forbidden energy and momentum triangles, thresholds, exact angular bounds, scalar phase-space endpoints and independent quadrature, binomial moments, Monte Carlo agreement and control cases. They bring the scientific/project suite from 393 to 422 tests.

The archived paper ArcSecs: A Physical-Process Research Program for Photon Propagation, Cosmic Distance, and Relational Inertia (Parts I–XXVIII), pp. 14–17, supplies the drag problem and the timing obstruction; Chapter 30R independently checked them. Chapter 30S is a newly derived bounded follow-on, not an inherited Part XXIX paper or a newly numbered historical report. For methodological context, [BS1] is a published review of threshold reactions. Neither the review nor these tests is evidence of the proposed bath in nature.

The next physical step is a positive-coefficient, gauge-invariant vector–bath interaction, with all polarization amplitudes, stimulated and inverse processes, and a joint kinetic transport equation for energy, momentum and angular distributions. Test the finite-gap and soft limits against the scalar benchmark before proceeding to an independently calibrated source and receiver, then a matter/regulator transport model and observational likelihood. Preserve the original 12-principle charter and all 41 source reports.

For the reference dimensionless AGE-H trajectory, the independent calculation gives arrival at 1.445830121453, final group speed 0.822103826, retained energy fraction 0.695302670, effective gap 0.506501369, heat 0.303414617 and receiver recoil energy 0.001282713. The energy and momentum residuals are about 2.53×10−112.53\times10^{-11} and 5.55×10−165.55\times10^{-16}, respectively. Twenty of the 21 audit cases arrive; one short-horizon control remains incomplete. Arrival is not a certificate of monotonic slowing, and a negative sampled derivative is not an interval proof. Finite-wall cases at masses 100, 10 and 1 are separate reduced controls. The substantial dressed gap and its detector response remain unresolved.

Part XXXIV (Section 15, equations K1–K14) investigates two physically distinct ways to preserve direction while radiation changes branch. A finite-range scalar mediator has a nonzero forward momentum-transfer floor when both final masses increase. In the illustrative large-gap reference, the formal long-range kernel accepts only about 9.33×10−119.33\times10^{-11} of converted packets within one arcsecond. This is not a successful beam-preserving aging law. A different phase-matched collective reservoir admits an exactly collinear, energy- and momentum-conserving conversion in a normalized example: incident energy 1, outgoing energy 0.895003493, reservoir energy 0.104996507 and outgoing group speed 0.829398767. The result presupposes selection of the appropriate physical reservoir mode; a finite isolated cell exhibits back-conversion. An open-cell escape model analytically gives monotone total converted population for κ≥4G\kappa\geq4G, but does not prove continuous slowing of an individual photon. The static-wall interval certificate applies only to the original AGE-H trajectory, not to a moving wall or microscopic interaction. The actual medium, coherence and spectral density, reverse reactions, conserved-current detection, clock calibration, C-01 emission ceiling and astronomical fit remain research objectives. These are contributor-reported conditional results, not new measurements or independently reproduced calculations.

Shared acceptance contract

C-01 requires an actual emission mechanism and a specified local reference. The bounded ballistic control in the review is causal by its assumed boost law, yet a packet may slow relative to matter while accelerating in common coordinates. It does not repair the older Chapter 32A advection model into a universal law. The regulator, matter, radiation and reservoir must have reciprocal dynamics, bounded energy, causal characteristics, an explicit boundary and a common calibrated detector. Impedance matching alone cannot establish unchanged atomic or nuclear rates.

For radiation transport, distinguish arrival-coordinate stretch, physical clock stretch and spectral shift. The optical flux ledger uses common time and energy standards, or explicitly calibrated local units. Require a derived spectrum, angular scattering, receiver response and energy recipient before fitting distances. Compare geometric anchors, angular maps, brightness and timing jointly; do not impose a size or distance reduction. Source values checked by the audit include the LMC eclipsing-binary distance and NGC 4258 maser distance, DES supernova timing and GW170817/GRB timing. These are independent constraints with their original assumptions. The named extreme-object dossiers still require primary-source verification and uncertainty budgets; conflicting classifications are not new distance measurements.
